I will estimate the causal effect of log household income per adult equivalent on reported illness episodes using an instrumental-variables panel design: transfer_draw (the 1993 random village draw for unconditional cash transfers) as an instrument for log income in 2SLS with individual fixed effects and survey-round fixed effects, clustering SEs at the village level and restricting the main IV sample to the six pilot-area villages where transfer_draw is observed. Key variables are the outcome (number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks), the endogenous treatment (log household income per adult equivalent), the instrument (transfer_draw), and covariates to improve precision and address time-varying confounding (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic, and season_rain); I will always report the reduced form, first-stage F-stat, and LATE interpretation. Because the published documentation reports a weak first-stage (F≈2) I will use weak-instrument–robust inference (Anderson–Rubin and LIML), report bounds, and present OLS, IV, and reduced-form estimates side-by-side. The main threat is that the instrument is both weak and has limited external validity (identifies compliers in three drawn vs three undrawn pilot villages), and there may be village-level spillovers, differential attrition or post-draw migration affecting health outcomes; I will run balance tests on pre-draw observables and placebo trend tests to probe these threats. Robustness checks will include excluding observations from months after anomalous rainfall, controlling flexibly for season_rain (since rainfall affects income and malaria), and sensitivity analyses that use alternative inference and sample definitions.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using panel two-stage least squares with individual and survey-round fixed effects, instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with assignment to the fund's 1993 draw (transfer_draw) interacted with a post-1993 indicator to isolate exogenous income changes from the unconditional cash transfers. The outcome is the respondent's count of illness episodes in the prior four weeks; key covariates will include age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic, and village-time controls, and standard errors will be clustered at the village level. I will report first-stage diagnostics, use weak-instrument-robust inference (e.g., Anderson-Rubin/CFi), and run robustness checks including within-individual (fixed-effects) estimates and IV limited to the six pilot villages. The main threat is that the instrument is weak (first-stage F ≈ 2), producing imprecise and potentially biased IV estimates and limiting external validity to compliers in the pilot area. Secondary concerns are spillovers between pilot and non-pilot villages and differential attrition after the draw, which I will test by balance and attrition analyses.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of log household income per adult equivalent on individual illness episodes using two-stage least squares (2SLS) with individual and survey-round fixed effects, instrumenting income with the random 1993 fund draw (transfer_draw) so identification comes from the quasi-random assignment of unconditional cash transfers to whole villages. Key variables are instrument = transfer_draw, treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, outcome = person-level count of illness episodes in the preceding four weeks; I will cluster standard errors at the village level and report weak-instrument-robust (Anderson–Rubin and LIML) confidence intervals. Because transfer_draw applies only to households in the six pilot-area villages and has a weak first stage (F≈2), I will present LATE estimates for the pilot area and avoid overgeneralizing to the whole region. I will control flexibly for time-varying village covariates and test for spillovers by excluding neighboring villages in sensitivity checks. The main threat is weak instruments/limited power and limited external validity (and potential spillovers), while an alternative candidate instrument—season_rain—predicts income but plausibly violates exclusion because rainfall directly affects malaria and other disease risk and so is not valid here.
CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will identify the causal effect using the 1993 randomized village-level draw of an unconditional cash transfer as an instrument for log household income, restricting the sample to households in the 6 pilot-area villages and exploiting within-household changes across survey rounds with individual and survey-round fixed effects. The outcome is the number of illness episodes reported in the prior four weeks, the endogenous treatment is log household income per adult equivalent, and the instrument is the randomized assignment to a drawn village (transfer_draw), implemented as the draw indicator interacted with a post-draw indicator in a difference-in-differences/IV framework. I will estimate two-stage least squares (first stage: income on transfer_draw×post plus fixed effects and time-varying covariates like age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres; second stage: illness on predicted income), cluster standard errors at the village level, and report ITT and LATE. Main threat: a weak first stage (F≈2) and very few clusters (3 treated villages) which can produce imprecise and potentially biased IV estimates, plus possible spillovers or differential pre-trends despite randomization. As robustness I will report the DiD ITT, show pre-trends, and (only for sensitivity) present results using season_rain as an alternative instrument while noting its direct effect on health.  
CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate a fuzzy IV (2SLS) identifying the local average causal effect of log household income per adult equivalent on illness episodes by exploiting the 1993 random village draw for the unconditional cash transfer (transfer_draw × post‑1993 indicator) as an instrument, with individual and survey‑round fixed effects and village‑clustered standard errors. The outcome is the self‑reported count of illness episodes in the prior four weeks; the endogenous regressor is log household income per adult equivalent; the instrument is assignment to a drawn village interacted with the post‑draw period. Because the outcome is a count I will present linear IV estimates and an IV‑Poisson/control‑function specification, and adjust precision with baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic) to improve efficiency and test balance. The main threat is a very weak first stage (the agency reports a first‑stage F ≈ 2 within the six‑village subsample), yielding imprecise or biased IV estimates and limited external validity; I will therefore report weak‑IV‑robust inference (AR, LIML), placebo checks, and bounds. If the instrument proves unusable I will fall back to individual fixed‑effects exploiting within‑person income variation but treat those estimates as associational because exogenous shocks like season_rain plausibly affect health directly.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | doubtful
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares (IV), using the 1993 randomized draw into the quarterly unconditional cash-transfer pilot (transfer_draw) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent, restricting to the six pilot-area villages and including individual and survey-round fixed effects and village-clustered standard errors. Key variables are treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, outcome = number of reported illness episodes in the past four weeks (estimated with IV-OLS and a Poisson IV check), instrument = transfer_draw, and covariates for precision such as age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic and season_rain. Identification rests on the random draw ensuring exogenous variation in income and the exclusion that transfer_draw affects health only through income; I will report first-stage diagnostics and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or LIML) if needed. The main threat is a weak first stage (reported F ≈ 2) plus limited external validity and potential violation of exclusion via spillovers, changes in health services, or differential reporting/attrition in drawn villages. I will present IV estimates with robust CIs and sensitivity checks (including restricting to pre/post-draw comparisons, placebo outcomes, and exploring season_rain as an alternative exogenous shock but not a primary instrument because rainfall plausibly affects health directly).
CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
land_acres | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will identify the causal effect using the 1993 random village draw for the unconditional quarterly cash transfer (transfer_draw) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent and estimate 2SLS with individual and survey-round fixed effects, clustering standard errors at the village level. Key variables are: endogenous treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, instrument = transfer_draw, outcome = number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks, with baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres) and village fixed effects as robustness controls. Because the outcome is count data I will present linear IV (2SLS) estimates plus IV-poisson or control-function robustness checks, and report weak-IV-robust confidence sets (Anderson–Rubin and CLR). The main threat is a weak first stage (first-stage F≈2) and possible spillovers or other village-level changes that violate the exclusion restriction, so I will (a) present ITT DiD estimates restricted to the six pilot villages, (b) run randomization inference and balance tests on pre-draw outcomes and covariates, and (c) test for spillovers and heterogeneous effects. If transfer_draw proves too weak or shows violations, I will report reduced-form ITT and refrain from claiming a precise LATE. CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
land_acres | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (IV) where season_rain (deviation from long-run average rainfall at the village station, scaled per 100 mm) instruments log household income per adult equivalent, estimating its effect on the number of self-reported illness episodes in the prior four weeks; models will include individual and survey-round fixed effects and village-clustered standard errors. Key variables are outcome = illness_count, endogenous regressor = log_income_per_adult_equivalent, instrument = season_rain, with controls age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres and pre-trend checks. I will check first-stage strength, report IV and reduced-form estimates, and conduct robustness checks using alternative rainfall windows and heterogeneity by farmed acres. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because rainfall may affect health directly (e.g., malaria, waterborne disease, or nutrition) or be correlated with other time-varying local shocks; I will test for direct pathways by controlling for plausible mediators, using placebo lags, and bounding approaches. Given the weak first-stage on the random transfer_draw (F≈2) I will not rely on it as the primary instrument but will report its diagnostics. If IV results are fragile I will present fixed-effects OLS with rich controls and sensitivity analyses as a complementary estimate.

CANDIDATES:
season_rain | plausible
transfer_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: season_rain

I will estimate the causal effect of log household income per adult equivalent on number of self-reported illness episodes using an instrumental-variables design that exploits the 1993 randomized draw of villages for the unconditional cash transfer: within the six pilot villages I will use the randomized draw (transfer_draw), interacted with a post-1993 indicator, as the instrument for log income in two-stage least squares. The first stage will regress log household income on the instrument, individual fixed effects, survey-round fixed effects, and time-varying covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, etc.), clustering standard errors at the village level; the second stage will regress illness episodes on the fitted values of income with the same fixed effects and covariates. Key variables are outcome = illness episodes in the past 4 weeks, treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, and instrument = transfer_draw (× post-1993). The main threat is a weak first stage (first-stage F ≈ 2) and limited external validity because only six pilot villages are randomized, plus potential spillovers or other concurrent changes in drawn villages that could violate the exclusion restriction; I will report weak-IV robust CIs, show pre-trends, and run placebo checks and sensitivity analyses excluding nearby villages.  
CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate a LATE for graduation on adult turnout using an IV (2SLS) design that exploits the 1965 elective-credit random draw (credit_waiver) as an instrument for graduating by age 19, restricting to the 1965 students who reached 12th grade. Key variables are: treatment = graduated_by_19, outcome = voted_any_general_1998_2008 (voter-file match), instrument = credit_waiver, and baseline covariates for precision (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home, birth_year). I will report the first-stage (share point change and F-stat), use weak-instrument-robust CIs (Anderson–Rubin/LIML), and present the ITT alongside IV estimates to show magnitudes. The main threat is a weak instrument (first-stage F≈2) producing imprecise or biased 2SLS estimates and limiting inference to compliers in the 1965 senior cohort; I also considered preschool_assign but exclude it because the preschool intervention plausibly has direct effects on adult turnout (violating exclusion). CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate a local average treatment effect of graduating from high school by age 19 on adult turnout using instrumental variables (2SLS) that exploit the district's randomized 1965 senior-year elective credit waiver as an instrument for graduation. Key variables are: instrument = credit_waiver (restricted to the 1965 cohort who reached 12th grade), endogenous treatment = graduated_by_19, outcome = voted in at least one general election 1998–2008 (voter-file match); I will include baseline covariates (birth_year, female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index) for precision and restrict the sample to non-missing instrument observations. I will report first-stage statistics (F) and use weak-instrument–robust inference (Anderson–Rubin and LIML) given the noted F≈2, and I will assess balance of observables by instrument to support randomization. The main threat is weak instrument inference and small sample size in the 1965 subsample (low power and wide CIs), plus any remaining concern that the waiver might affect turnout through channels other than graduation despite the memo's claim that it "changed nothing else." CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect by 2SLS using randomized assignment to the district preschool program (preschool_assign) as an instrument for graduating high school by age 19, so the estimate is the LATE for compliers; robust SEs and cohort fixed effects will be used. Key variables are the binary outcome voted_1998_2008 (voted in any general election 1998–2008), the binary treatment graduated_by_19, the instrument preschool_assign, and baseline covariates female, iq_entry, parent_educ, father_home, ses_index, and birth_year (included to improve precision and check balance). I will report first-stage statistics (F-stat), conduct balance tests on baseline variables, and run placebo and intermediate-outcome tests; in sensitivity analyses I will use the 1965 credit_waiver as a secondary instrument (only for that cohort) and compare IV to OLS and bounding approaches. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction and differential attrition/matching: preschool_assign may affect turnout directly via long-run non-schooling channels (or affect probability of being matched to voter files), so I will present robustness checks, bounds, and transparent discussion of assumptions.  
CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | plausible
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: preschool_assign

Identify the causal effect via two-stage least squares (IV) using the district's randomized 1965 elective-credit waiver as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19, estimating the LATE for compliers in the 1965 senior cohort. Key variables are: endogenous treatment = graduated_by_19 (binary), outcome = voted_in_any_general_1998_2008 (from voter-file matches), instrument = credit_waiver (1965 subsample), and baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year, father_home) for precision and balance checks. Because the waiver's first stage is weak (≈4 percentage-point increase; F≈2) I will report weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin), LIML, first-stage and reduced-form estimates, and emphasize the LATE interpretation limited to the 1965 compliers. I will run balance tests on baseline covariates by waiver draw, and conduct sensitivity analyses that (a) use preschool_assign as an alternative instrument in supplementary analyses and (b) present partial-identification bounds if exclusion is suspect. The main threat is instrument weakness and limited external validity (imprecise IV estimates and an effect that generalizes only to compliers in the 1965 cohort); if the waiver is too weak I will present intent-to-treat estimates from preschool_assign as a complementary analysis but treat those estimates cautiously because preschool_assign plausibly affects turnout through non-graduation pathways (psychosocial skills), violating exclusion for the graduation effect.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares (2SLS) using random assignment to the two-year preschool program (preschool_assign) as an instrument for graduating high school by age 19, so the estimate identifies a LATE for compliers; I will also report the ITT (reduced form) for transparency. The outcome is the indicator for voting in at least one general election 1998–2008 from the public voter file, the endogenous treatment is graduated_by_19, and I will include baseline covariates for precision (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home, birth_year) while preserving the randomized instrument. I will report first-stage strength (F-stat), run weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or conditional likelihood) given N=123, and present both 2SLS point estimates and robust CIs. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: preschool_assign may affect adult turnout through channels other than high-school graduation (long-run cognitive, socialization, later schooling, or differential probability of being matched in the voter file) or differential attrition/missingness. To address this I will test balance on baseline covariates by instrument, run placebo outcome checks, estimate bounds and sensitivity analyses, and use credit_waiver as a secondary (subsample) robustness check despite its weak first stage. I will interpret results as causal for compliers and be explicit about limited external validity and any DUA-driven suppression of small cell estimates.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | plausible
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: preschool_assign

I will estimate a LATE using the randomized 1965 district credit_waiver as an instrument for graduating high school by age 19 in a fuzzy IV (2SLS) framework among the subsample to whom the waiver applied, and report the ITT alongside IV estimates. Key variables are instrument = credit_waiver, endogenous treatment = graduated_by_19, outcome = voted_in_any_general_1998_2008 (voter-file match), and baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year) to improve precision; I will restrict the sample to 1965-wave students who reached 12th grade and use robust/clustered SEs. Because the waiver first-stage is weak (≈4 percentage points, F≈2) I will rely on weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin, LIML, robust CIs), report compliance rates, and present bounds/sensitivity analyses. The main threat is weak instrument combined with small sample and limited external validity (identifies compliers in one cohort), although the program memo states the waiver "changed nothing else," which supports the exclusion restriction but cannot be fully tested.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

Use the study’s randomized preschool assignment as an instrumental variable and estimate the local average treatment effect (LATE) of graduating high school by age 19 on adult voter turnout via two-stage least squares (2SLS).  Specify the first stage as graduated_by_19 = α + π·preschool_assign + γ·(baseline covariates) + u and the second stage as voted_1998_2008 = β·graduated_hat + δ·(baseline covariates) + ε.  Key variables are graduated_by_19 (treatment), voted_in_1998_2008 (outcome from voter files), instrument = preschool_assign, and baseline covariates for precision (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year).  Because the sample is small (n=123), report weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or similar), use robust standard errors and randomization inference where feasible, and present the reduced-form as well as 2SLS estimates.  The main threat to identification is violation of the exclusion restriction — preschool_assign may affect adult turnout through non-education channels (civic socialization, networks, or other long-term treatment effects) or differential attrition/matching to voter files.  As a robustness check consider the 1965 credit_waiver random draw within that cohort (weak first stage) and compare reduced-form and bounds estimates.  
CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | plausible
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: preschool_assign

I will estimate the causal effect using instrumental variables (2SLS) exploiting the district's randomized elective-credit draw (credit_waiver) among the 1965 senior wave as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19, restricting to that cohort so the instrument's randomization is respected. The key variables are credit_waiver (instrument), graduated_by_19 (endogenous treatment), and voted_any_1998_2008 (binary outcome from voter files); I will include baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year) to improve precision and check robustness. Because documentation reports a weak first stage (~4 percentage points, F≈2) I will present reduced-form estimates, IV estimates with weak‑IV‑robust inference (Anderson–Rubin, LIML), and report first‑stage statistics and sensitivity/bounds for the LATE. I will run balance and differential‑attrition checks by the draw, placebo outcomes the waiver should not affect, and use preschool_assign as a negative control to probe exclusion. The main threat is instrument weakness (low first‑stage F and small subsample) producing imprecise and fragile IV inference and limited external validity to the 1965 seniors; secondary threats are any unrecorded channels by which the waiver could have affected turnout or differential voter‑file match rates. If the waiver proves unusably weak I will report reduced‑form ITT effects and be explicit that no credible instrument is available in this data for the full sample. 

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate a local average treatment effect using two-stage least squares (IV) where randomized preschool assignment (preschool_assign) instruments for the binary treatment "graduated from high school by age 19" to identify the effect on the binary outcome "voted in at least one general election, 1998–2008"; this leverages randomization to avoid simple selection bias. Key variables are: instrument = preschool_assign, endogenous regressor = graduated_by_19, outcome = voted_any_1998_2008, and baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year) will be included for precision and to demonstrate balance. I will report first-stage strength (F-statistic), estimate complier characteristics, use robust SEs, and run sensitivity checks including bounds/partial-identification and alternative estimators (e.g., IV with limited-information likelihood). The main threat to identification is violation of the exclusion restriction: preschool_assign plausibly affects adult turnout through channels other than completing high school (improved socioemotional and civic-related skills), so the IV estimate may not isolate only the schooling effect; secondary threats are voter-file match error and heterogeneous attrition. Because credit_waiver applies only to a 1965 senior subset and has a very weak first stage (F≈2), I will not rely on it as the primary instrument but will use it in robustness checks where appropriate.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | doubtful
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: preschool_assign

I will estimate the causal effect with two-stage least squares (2SLS) using the count of waterways crossing a city as an instrument for the city's segregation index, including state-by-year fixed effects and clustering standard errors at the state level; first stage and reduced-form tests, plus weak-instrument diagnostics, will be reported. The outcome is direct general expenditure per resident (deflated dollars) and the treatment is the multigroup entropy segregation index (0–100); baseline controls will include log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and region, and I will show OLS and IV point estimates for comparison. The instrument is justified because waterways are historical geographic features that the codebook documents raise segregation by about 1.5 points each and are plausibly exogenous to modern policy choices. I will test the exclusion by checking whether waterways predict other channels (e.g., measures of fragmentation, number of overlapping jurisdictions, or infrastructure spending) and by running placebo outcomes and heterogeneity by municipal fragmentation. The main credible threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: waterways may directly affect per-capita spending through municipal fragmentation, flood/infrastructure costs, or historical boundary rules, which would bias the IV estimate. If exclusion appears violated or the first stage is weak, I will report bounds (e.g., IV with limited-exogeneity sensitivity) and present the OLS as a robustness benchmark.  
CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate a causal effect using two-stage least squares that instruments the city's segregation index with the number of waterways crossing the city, exploiting the panel of ~2,600 cities across four census years and including city fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects. The first stage regresses the multigroup entropy segregation index on waterways and covariates (log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region indicators), and the second stage regresses direct general expenditure per resident on the predicted segregation from that first stage. I will cluster standard errors at the city level, report the first-stage F-statistic, and run falsification tests (placebo outcomes, leads of the instrument) and sensitivity analyses. Key variables are: treatment = segregation index, outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars), instrument = waterways, and controls as listed above; I will also evaluate audit_grant as an alternative instrument limited to its defined subsample. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if waterways directly affect public spending (e.g., flood control, infrastructure, parks) or capture unobserved geographic confounders; I will test robustness by adding waterways-related spending proxies and geographic controls and by restricting samples.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate a two-stage least-squares IV model using the number of waterways that cross a city as an instrument for the city's multigroup entropy segregation index, including state-by-year fixed effects and controls for log_pop. Key variables are: outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars), treatment = segregation index (0–100), instrument = waterways, and covariates = pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region and other city characteristics from the codebook. Identification exploits the documented mechanical effect of waterways (≈1.5 index points per additional waterway) on segregation while assuming that, after conditioning on covariates and state-by-year shocks, waterways do not affect per-capita municipal spending except through segregation. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction — waterways may directly change spending needs or local economic structure (flood control, bridges, parks) or proxy for historical settlement patterns correlated with unobserved determinants of spending; I will address this with balance tests, placebo outcomes, geography/infrastructure controls, and sensitivity analyses. I considered the randomized audit_grant as an alternative instrument but will not use it as the primary instrument because it applies to only 40 large cities and has a weak first stage (F≈2); I will report it only as a robustness check.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate the causal effect of segregation on per‑resident direct general expenditure using two‑stage least squares: first stage regresses the city's multigroup entropy segregation index on the count of historical waterways crossing the city (the instrument) plus controls and state-by-year fixed effects, and the second stage regresses expenditures per resident on the predicted segregation from the first stage. Key variables are: treatment = multigroup entropy segregation index (0–100), instrument = waterways (number of rivers/streams crossing the city), outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars); controls will include log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region and other covariates. The identifying assumption is that waterways are an exogenous, historical determinant of municipal boundary formation and thus segregation but do not directly affect modern city spending except through segregation. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if waterways directly influence current fiscal outcomes (e.g., via flood/infrastructure costs or persistent economic geography correlated with tax base); I will assess this with balance tests, controls for water‑related channels, placebo outcomes, and weak‑instrument diagnostics. If waterways fail validity or strength checks I will not rely on IV and will report bounds and sensitivity analyses instead.
CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
tax_base_002 | violated
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate the causal effect with two-stage least squares (2SLS), instrumenting the city's segregation index (multigroup entropy 0–100) with the exogenous count of waterways crossing the city, and include state-by-year fixed effects and controls for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, and region. First stage: segregationit = α + β·waterwaysit + γ·Xit + δst + εit; second stage: expenditure_per_residentit = π + θ·ŝegregationit + λ·Xit + δst + υit, clustering SEs at the state level. I will report instrument strength (first-stage F), use LIML if the instrument is weak, and as a robustness check run reduced-form estimates and a subsample IV using audit_grant among the 40 eligible cities. Key variables are treatment = segregation index, outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars), instrument = waterways, with controls and state-by-year fixed effects. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: waterways may directly affect municipal spending (flood control, bridges, parks, or development patterns) or proxy for other omitted geographic determinants of spending; I will probe this by controlling for observable waterways-related spending proxies, testing pre-trends, and reporting bounds if exclusion is doubtful. If waterways proves invalid or weak, I will present reduced-form and bounding estimates and be explicit that causal interpretation is limited.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate the causal effect of city racial segregation (multigroup entropy index, 0–100) on direct general expenditure per resident (dollars) using two-stage least squares, instrumenting segregation with the historical count of rivers/streams crossing the city (waterways). The first stage predicts segregation from waterways controlling for log_pop and time-varying city covariates (pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate) and including state-by-year fixed effects; the second stage regresses per-resident direct general expenditure on the predicted segregation, with standard errors clustered at the state level. Waterways plausibly exogenously influenced the drawing of municipal and school district boundaries (and thereby segregation) while being pre-determined relative to contemporary budgeting decisions once we condition on observed covariates and state×year shocks. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if waterways directly affect current public spending (flood control, bridges/transport costs, parks, or local tax base) or proxy for other persistent geographic or economic factors; I will probe this with balance tests, geographic controls, placebo outcomes, and weak-instrument diagnostics.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: waterways

I will estimate the effect of the city's segregation (multigroup entropy index, 0–100) on real direct general expenditure per resident using two-stage least squares that instruments segregation with the city's number of waterways, exploiting cross-city variation in four census years and including state-by-year fixed effects. The first stage predicts segregation from waterways plus controls (log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region and year dummies); the second stage regresses inflation-adjusted direct general expenditure per resident on predicted segregation. I will cluster standard errors at the state or metro level, report first-stage F-statistics and weak-IV-robust confidence intervals, and present reduced-form and placebo tests (outcomes unlikely to respond to segregation) and an alternative-IV check using audit_grant in the restricted large-city subsample. The key variables are: treatment = segregation index, outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (CPI-deflated), instrument = waterways, and covariates as listed above. The identifying assumption is that waterways affect city spending only through their effect on segregation conditional on controls and state-by-year shocks. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because waterways plausibly affect local spending directly (flood control, bridges, parks) or via municipal fragmentation; I will probe and report sensitivity analyses and bounds if this cannot be ruled out.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | plausible
audit_grant | doubtful
